transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-02-07 16:00 UTC | Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Moreno (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood CSM); Evan Torres (SparkPay CTO), Priya Desai (SparkPay Backend), Olga Kuznetsov (SparkPay Security), Samir Patel (SparkPay SRE)

--- Auto-generated summary (brief) ---
Maya (Redwood): Quick demo of hosted chat + resilience patterns. Walk through console, streaming params, retries, and Optimize suggestions. Customer asks about PCI/data residency, private deployment options, and benchmarking.

Topics covered: streaming vs sync, tokenization and prompt chunking, max_tokens/temperature/top_p, retry backoff strategies, prefix caching/KV cache behavior, failovers to lower-cost model variant, console trace and per-route metrics, Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization.

--- Transcript ---
00:00 Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
00:04 Evan (SparkPay): yes loud and clear, thanks Maya. good to meet you all.
00:10 Maya: awesome, yeah so quick runbook for today, we'll do about 35 minutes of demo, Luca will run through streaming and params and some failure-mode examples, then leave time for security questions and next steps. does that sound good?
00:21 Priya D: sounds good. Evan nodded.
00:25 Luca (Redwood SE): yeah i'll focus on live behavior and show console traces — you'll see token-level latency and where batching helps. also we'll kick off a simple retry to show backoff patterns.
00:35 Olga (SparkPay Security): quick heads up — we have PCI constraints around payment data and we need to understand where logs and inputs live, encryption at rest, and whether anything is stored in third-party logs.
00:48 Maya: totally, we'll cover that briefly and follow up with the security pack. short answer: hosted keeps only ephemeral input by default, we have options for retention and redaction and integrations with customer KMS for key management. we'll send the SOC2 and ISO docs after the call.
01:05 Samir (SRE): also curious about SLOs — how predictable is latency for concurrent sessions?
01:11 Luca: great Q. latency depends on model choice, concurrency, and batching. for hosted API we surface per-route latency p50/p95 in the console. to keep it predictable you can pin a model variant and enable dedicated capacity; for hosted we'll show how the runtime adjusts batching and the effect on tail latency.
01:30 Maya: ok jumping into the console — i'll share my screen.
01:37 [screen share starts - console view] 
01:45 Luca: here is a simple chat session in the sandbox. note the stream mode — you get partial tokens as they generate. streaming is great for perceived latency but if you have strict ordering requirements or idempotency you may want sync responses or the conversations API with checkpoints.
02:05 Luca: watch the tokens stream in the network tab, and over here the per-token timings — we expose the kernel selection and kv-cache hits, though sometimes the transcription reads that as 'KV cash' in older exports, haha.
02:20 Priya D: can you demo an interruption? like connection drop and resume?
02:25 Luca: sure. i'll start a stream and then force a network interruption — you'll see the client can reconnect and request the remainder using the conversation id; if you prefer strictly idempotent calls, we also return a partial response and a way to re-ask with the same prefix.
02:40 [streaming demo started] 
02:48 Luca: okay killing the connection now — and rejoining — see the SDK resumes and resumes token delivery, there is a small re-fetch to ensure no tokens lost.
03:05 Evan: interesting, do you do any automatic dedupe or is that on the client?
03:09 Luca: mostly client-side dedupe. we provide idempotency keys and sequence markers. for long-running chats you typically checkpoint and server-side we maintain a short-term kv-cache for prefix hits that avoids re-computation.
03:28 Samir: about retries — we see transient 503s from our infra sometimes. what's your recommended backoff?
03:33 Luca: we recommend exponential backoff with jitter, and a max of 3 retries for interactive flows. for high-volume async batches you can be more aggressive with queueing. also we expose retriable error classes in the SDK so you can tune for your error surface.
03:50 Priya D: does retry count cause extra cost?
03:54 Maya: yes retries that re-generate tokens can increase cost — that's why the prefix caching and the ability to resume from a conversation checkpoint are useful: they minimize re-generation. Optimize will later suggest caching thresholds based on your traffic profile.
04:10 Olga: about PII — if a customer message contains card numbers, what's Redwood's stance? do you enable PII redaction?
04:18 Maya: by default, we recommend client-side redaction for card numbers, but we also offer server-side redactors and a pre-tokenization hook. for regulated customers we can also provide private deployment or bring-your-own-key so logs never leave your VPC. we'll include the redaction guide in the security pack.
04:40 Luca: switching gears to generation params — temp, top_p, max_output_tokens, and stop sequences. small temp keeps responses deterministic — good for payment confirmations. higher temp increases variability which is useful for creative responses but not for transaction language.
05:00 Luca: demonstration now — lower temperature, set max_output_tokens 60, show fewer hallucinations, and then warm temp to show more varied wording.
05:18 [demo generates two responses side-by-side] 
05:28 Priya D: that side-by-side view is helpful. does the console show token cost breakdown?
05:32 Luca: yes, per-request and cumulative token usage, and our Optimize tab gives model/quantization recs to lower per-token cost. for example, for short confirmations we sometimes recommend a smaller model variant quantized to int8 to save cost while keeping latency low.
05:48 Evan: about model variants — if capacity is constrained, can you fallback? we don't want timeouts in checkout flows.
05:55 Maya: we have automated fallback policies — route requests to a compatible variant or region if latency breaches SLOs. you can configure a prioritized policy: primary model, then fallback model, then an error policy. fallback is helpful, but you should test that variant for acceptance.
06:14 Samir: can fallbacks cause behavior changes we don't expect?
06:18 Luca: yes which is why we recommend canarying fallbacks with A/B tests — the console supports rollouts and per-route evaluation so you can compare outputs across variants.
06:28 Olga: security again — KMS, HSM support?
06:31 Maya: yes we integrate with customer KMS for private keys; for on-prem/private deployment we support HSM for added compliance. full details in the security pack.
06:40 Priya D: can you show a quick Optimize suggestion for our sample workload?
06:44 Luca: i have a small mock profile here — mostly short confirmative messages, lots of concurrent small chats. Optimize suggests aggressive prefix/KV caching, reduce max tokens, batch small requests for micro-bursts, and consider a quantized model for inference.
07:05 [Optimize suggestions shown: caching, batching thresholds, quantization level] 
07:20 Priya D: curious about batching — doesn't that increase latency??
07:24 Luca: good point. batching improves throughput and cost but can increase tail latency. Redwood's runtime uses smart batching with latency SLOs — it will cap batch wait times and flush early if latency is approaching target. you can set per-route latency or cost preference.
07:44 Evan: is there a way to see per-token latency on production traces?
07:48 Luca: yes per-request traces show token timelines and kernel choices. we also surface batch composition and queue wait time so you can see where the time is spent.
07:58 Samir: one of our pain points: idempotent webhooks calling the LLM — any guidance?
08:02 Luca: use idempotency keys, store conversation checkpoints, and avoid retries that re-generate large outputs. for webhooks you can pre-render deterministic confirmations with low temp and short max tokens to make retries safe.
08:20 Maya: ok quick failure-mode demo — i'll throttle the backend and show retry policy in action.
08:26 [demo: throttle induced, SDK logs show retries, then fallback to a smaller model variant] 
08:40 Priya D: i noticed an earlier export called 'KV cash' in a transcript; will that be confusing in logs?
08:45 Luca: haha that's just transcription sillyness — in the console it's 'KV cache' everywhere. the export might corrupt some names but not the structured logs.
08:52 Olga: on data residency — we need EU-only data for EU customers. can hosted do region-restricted storage?
08:58 Maya: yes we can pin requests to region and the hosted control plane has region-aware routing. for strict EU-only cases we often recommend the Private deployment, but we do offer hosted region compliance options.
09:12 Evan: timeline — we want to pilot within Q2, production later. what does onboarding look like?
09:17 Priya Singh (CSM): onboarding: trial tenant, security review, benchmark run, then pilot agreement for dedicated pools if needed. typically 4–8 weeks for pilot to production depending on compliance.
09:32 Maya: thanks all. recap: we'll provision a trial tenant, send security docs, Luca will prepare benchmark scripts, and we'll schedule the benchmark in early March.
09:44 Evan: sounds good.
09:48 Maya: any final Qs?
09:51 Priya D: none from me.
09:52 Olga: please include redaction best practices in the pack.
09:55 Maya: will do. thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with calendar invites and the security pack.
09:59 [call ends]

--- End of transcript ---
